In the city by the river, the great bridge would begin to move.
Bridges like this are built to sway a little in a storm.
Not like this.
The deck would swing from side to side, like a ribbon.
By now, the streets would be empty.
Everyone would be sheltering indoors.
Parked cars would be lifted and thrown.
Three hundred and twenty.
As strong as the most violent tornadoes.
Chimneys and balconies would break away.
Trees would be stripped bare.
Four hundred and fifty.
Faster than any gust ever measured on the surface of the Earth.
The air would be thick with dust.
You could barely see across the river.
The old water tower would lean, and then fall.
Out on the bridge, the steel cables would begin to snap.
Each one would crack like a gunshot.
Six hundred.
Eight hundred.
Faster than a passenger jet.
One thousand kilometers per hour.
Almost the speed of sound.
In the real world, no wind could last like this.
Every storm runs out of energy.
Every storm ends.
And that is the only reason our cities are still standing.
